analysis_notes.good_evil_mirror_note: Torah #151 has a clear good/evil mirror structure operating on two axes: (1) AXIS OF VAV: Package 1 (וָאו/חִיּוּת, good: the life-force present in its fullness) mirrors Package 2's חֶסְרוֹן חִיּוּת (evil: the life-force absent). This is the most direct good/evil mirror in the Torah. (2) AXIS OF THE MOON: Package 3 (לְבָנָה in her tikkun/filling aspect, good: the moon being rectified, providing atonement) mirrors Package 2's פְּגִימַת הַלְּבָנָה (evil: the moon in her blemished/deficient state, causing death in children). The node לְבָנָה bridges both packages — it appears as the deficient moon (evil, Package 2) and the filling moon (good, Package 3). This dual-membership is the classic good/evil bridge structure described in framework.md.
analysis_notes.structural_note: Torah #151 is extremely compact (6 lines) but contains a richly structured kabbalistic argument: a segulah (practical remedy) is explained through a chain of bechina identifications that establish why Rosh Chodesh heals children. The zero-bechina situation in the dataset is a coverage gap. Five bechina pairs are present in the text. The teaching's entire conceptual architecture rests on the vav = life-force equation (addition #1), which is both the positive pole (Package 1) and, in its absence, the evil pole (Package 2 via addition #3). The tikkun (Package 3) operates by correcting the moon's deficiency (Package 2) and flowing atonement/life to children.
